entries.speaker: Ana Pranger
entries.abstract: Courts promote family mediation as a cheaper, less adversarial alternative to litigated divorce, even mandating it in some jurisdictions and cases, but large-scale, causal evidence of its effects are lacking. Mediation may lower the costs of dissolution, as it does not require expensive lawyers or time before a judge. However, without strong evidence of mediation’s impact on outcomes, the net effect over couples and children is ambiguous, with implications for how income, assets, and responsibility for children are allocated across newly formed households. In this project, we leverage differences in mediation orders and mandates across judges and jurisdictions to identify the causal impact of going to mediation on dissolving couples and the court system. Using docket-level data on divorce cases in several localities and a judge fixed-effects design, we can isolate the causal effect of mediation on case characteristics and outcomes post-divorce. Preliminary results from Harris County, Texas, indicate that mediation leads cases to close more quickly, but may not lower observable contention. As the project progresses, we hope to connect these cases to compliance with child custody obligations, parenting and custody arrangements, and other downstream outcomes for courts, couples, and children.

entries.seminar_title: When Amazon Comes to Town: Warehouse Entry and Painkiller Consumption
entries.speaker: Alina Gafanova
entries.abstract: Amazon is the second largest private employer in the US. While economists have studied the effects of Amazon on workers’ wages and employment in local labor markets, there is little work on its effects on non-wage amenities. Amazon warehouses report 70% more injuries per worker than other warehouses, and there is anecdotal evidence that workers experience chronic pain and cope with it using over-the-counter painkillers. In this project, I use local painkiller sales to study whether the opening of an Amazon fulfillment center affects workers’ health beyond reported injuries.

entries.speaker: Cuimin Ba
entries.abstract: This paper studies persuasive behavior when the sender can both control the information the receiver observes (the message) and propose a model of its interpretation (the narrative). We show that the sender can manipulate the receiver into always taking her preferred action, even when they start with a correctly specified model of her strategic behavior, update by Bayes’ rule given their model, and are skeptical of her narrative. The key mechanism highlights a strong complementarity between strategic communication of information and narratives, which allows the sender to strictly outperform Bayesian persuasion without commitment power. We fully characterize the sender-optimal equilibrium for a broad class of information technologies. Softer information lowers the bar for full manipulation, while harder information expands the set of environments where any manipulation is possible. The results pro vide a formal foundation for understanding the widespread success of disinformation.
